extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory; constitutional designers and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading of constitutional principles comparing monarchy, aristocracy, democracy, and mixed government; extracts criteria for designing institutions that preserve liberty, reward merit, and prevent corruption or tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit absolute power in degree and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Power continued without proper limits produces tyranny; continuation of power is not itself the problem, but absolute/unlimited power corrupts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: "it was not barely continuation of power, it was absolute power, that did the mischief. If the power had been properly limited in degree, it might have been continued, without limitation of time... though it might be better to limit it, both in degree and in time." Use institutional limits (both in scope and duration) to prevent corruption from continued tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a plenary executive to prevent assembly–military conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a plenary (full) executive power, the senate and assembly would soon be at war and the victorious army's leader would become master of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that an annual assembly of representatives is ineffectual without a strong executive: "without a plenary executive power in the consul, the senate and assembly would soon be at war, and the leader of the victorious army master of the state." Ensure the executive can act decisively to avoid military usurpation and factional deadlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a mixed government with separated elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed constitution (monarchical, aristocratical, democratical elements) produces active emulation and sustains public spirit, public works, and good appointments over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises the mixture: it "edged men's spirits with an active emulation, and raised them to a lofty pitch of design and action." It cites Roman examples where mixed government supported excellence. Design institutions to balance the three elements rather than concentrate sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating sovereign power in one assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: When whole power is in one assembly, favorites will be continued by majority wishes and fundamental laws or oaths against it will be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: "a favourite will be continued in power whenever the majority wishes it, and every conceivable fundamental law, or even oath, against it will be dispensed with." Guard against permanent majority domination by structural checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open road to preferment encourages merit but needs institutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing advancement from all classes ('the road to preferment lies plain to every man') fosters emulation and increases chances that merit prevails, but this must be paired with safeguards against bribery and popular corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recognizes the advantage: "The chance for merit to prevail is greater than in any other." Yet it also cautions that open access can be abused; combine openness with accountability and filtering mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive appointment plus ministerial responsibility yields better appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: When the executive appoints offices and ministers are responsible for their exercise of power, appointments are made more cautiously and responsibly than by a single representative assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From: "the executive having the appointment to all offices... they are more cautious; they are responsible to their master for the recommendations they give, and to the nation and its representatives for the appointments that are made: whereas a single representative assembly is accountable to nobody." Design appointment processes that attach responsibility and reputational/institutional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single representative assembly lacks effective accountability for national offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a single assembly answer only to local constituents; the practical penalty is only electoral defeat, and constituents often know little about national officers, producing weak oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "each member is accountable to his constituents ... the penalty? No other than not to vote for him at the next election... constituents know nor care anything about any offices or officers but such as lie within the limits of their parish." Avoid relying solely on electoral punishment as the main check on national decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base constitutional design on rare exemplary individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions should not assume a steady supply of disinterested, magnanimous characters (Cincinnatus, Regulus); such virtues are rare and cannot be the foundation of durable institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns: "he who shall build his frame of government upon a presumption that characters of this stamp will arise in succession... will find himself mistaken." Design on realistic human incentives, not exceptional virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate public servants adequately
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who labour for the public should be supported by the public so they are not forced into poverty by service ("the labourer is worthy of his hire").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Regulus' case, the text argues that expecting public servants to serve while being left destitute is unreasonable and corrosive. Provide material support and honorable provision for public service to ensure capable people serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against popular prejudice, superstition, and name-based hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: Public judgment can be intoxicated with prejudice or superstition (e.g., blind hatred of 'king' as a word), which can produce irrational constitutional choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: "if nations and peoples cannot be brought to a more rational way of thinking... they will be the dupes of the designing." Institutional design should rely on reasoned principles, not popular word-aversion or prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: A standing senate or aristocratic body can defend public honour and check popular excess
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate as a standing power can protect the state from ingratitude, popular avarice, and unjust exclusions, acting as a long-term guardian of public dignity and continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cincinnatus and Paulus Aemilius' appointments and protection came from the senate. The text argues the senate saved the honour and dignity of the republic in several cases. Consider a durable deliberative body to check transient popular license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of annual election turning offices into mere tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Making an office annually elective can reduce its effective power to a tool of a dominant body (e.g., the senate) and render it incapable of protecting weaker classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From: "it was made annually elective... and became accordingly a mere tool of the senate, wholly defective of any power or will to protect plebeians." Consider the interaction of term length, re-election incentives, and institutional independence when designing offices.
